title: Germany’s second China shock – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: ECFR podcast episode (recorded August 12, 2026) frames a 'China shock 2.0' — driven by Chinese industrial overcapacity and state-backed manufacturing strength — as hitting German car manufacturing, chemicals and machine tools, causing job losses that are destabilising German coalition politics ahead of September 2026 regional elections.

insights.claim: A second wave of Chinese industrial competition ('China shock 2.0'), driven by manufacturing overcapacity and state-backed industrial strength, is hitting German car manufacturing, chemicals and machine-tools sectors and causing mounting job losses.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard, Janka Oertel, Andrew Small
insights.so_what: Signals continued downside pressure on German industrial employment and margins in autos, chemicals and machine tools — sectors to watch for further Chinese import penetration data.

insights.claim: The economic pain from Chinese competition is reshaping German domestic politics, exposing divisions within the governing coalition and putting pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz ahead of Germany's potentially divisive September 2026 regional elections.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard, Janka Oertel, Andrew Small
insights.so_what: Political risk factor for German coalition stability and policy continuity around September 2026 regional elections.

insights.claim: Policymakers in Brussels and European capitals are weighing responses ranging from emergency trade measures to new industrial strategies, framed as a trade-off between protecting Europe's industrial base and risking a damaging trade escalation with China.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard, Janka Oertel, Andrew Small
insights.so_what: Watch for EU trade-defence measures (tariffs, anti-dumping actions) versus industrial-policy responses as the two competing policy tracks likely to be debated over the coming months.

insights.claim: The episode raises an open question of whether Germany, given its own internal political turbulence, can still lead a coherent European response to Chinese industrial competition.
insights.speaker: Mark Leonard, Janka Oertel, Andrew Small
insights.so_what: Germany's capacity to lead EU-China trade policy is itself uncertain, which could delay or weaken any coordinated EU response.

source_meta.author: Mark Leonard, Janka Oertel, Andrew Small
